title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks

domain: differential equations in science and engineering
why_it_matters: the equation penalty steers the fit toward answers that obey physics, filling gaps where measurements are missing without pretending data alone tells the whole story
keeps: neural network guess plus a check that penalizes breaking the known equation that governs the system
leaves_out: it cannot fix a wrong equation, bad boundary conditions, or spots where the real answer has sharp jumps
failure_boundary: the penalty term hides small errors near boundaries, in thin layers, or where the real solution changes suddenly
everyday_anchor: Imagine tracing the path of a dropped ball from blurry photos—you'd see only a few points. A PINN is like saying: fit a curve through those dots, but make sure it obeys gravity at every step. The equation acts as a hidden guide that fills in the gaps.

title: Partial Differential Equations
common_problem: a quantity changes over space and time, so one number is not enough to describe what's happening
domain: fluids, heat, waves, mechanics, chemistry, climate, and other changing fields
why_it_matters: scientists use PDEs to write down laws of nature before machine learning enters, and they force you to be explicit about what you assume and what you skip
keeps: a field (a map of values across space), how those values shift with time and space, and boundary conditions to start the calculation
leaves_out: unmodeled forces, unresolved small-scale detail, uncertain parameters, and numerical error from discretization
failure_boundary: when data or learning skips the actual PDE constraints, it can ignore boundary conditions or conservation laws that the PDE was always enforcing
everyday_anchor: A weather map shows temperature, wind, and pressure at every location—and it changes hour by hour. A PDE is the rulebook that says how those values spread and push on each other. If you only watch the map without the rules, you might predict rain in the wrong place because you missed how pressure systems actually move.

title: Operator Learning
common_problem: engineers need to predict all the fields (temperature, pressure, flow) across a space and time for many input cases, not just one
domain: fast prediction for families of scientific simulations
why_it_matters: it trades solving expensive equations many times for one fast learned map, but only when new cases stay inside the training family
keeps: a learned function that maps any input condition (forcing, initial state, boundary) directly to a complete solution field
leaves_out: whether the learned map holds for new resolutions, geometries, or physics that look different from the training data
failure_boundary: the learned map produces plausible-looking fields that actually violate the physics or break when you shift the geometry
everyday_anchor: Imagine a chef learning to taste a single recipe's temperature at one point and then guessing the full heat throughout the oven. Operator learning does that across space—it learns to predict a complete field (temperature everywhere) from input conditions, becoming a shortcut for expensive simulations. But like the guessing chef, it only works reliably when the oven is the same shape and size as the ones it learned from.

title: Scientific Machine Learning
common_problem: predictions must obey the physical laws that define the problem, not just fit the data
domain: using data-driven models inside scientific workflows
why_it_matters: the neural network feels both the data AND the physics equations, so it learns the true rule and works on new cases the data never saw before
keeps: a neural network that learns by evaluating itself at test points and minimizing how far off it gets
leaves_out: any laws or checks the scientist does not write down as equations
failure_boundary: if no clear equation or boundary condition exists, the network learns the data shape but not the underlying rule
everyday_anchor: Imagine teaching a student to solve a maze by showing them photos of solved mazes, but also teaching them the rule "always keep your right hand on the wall." The rule helps them solve new mazes they never saw before. Scientific ML is the same: the neural network learns from data, but the physics equation guides it to find the true pattern, not just memorize.

title: Surrogate Modeling
common_problem: running a full simulation is too expensive to do for every design choice or question
why_it_matters: it speeds up repeated decisions in design or control when the cost of the real simulator would stop progress, but can hide missing physics if pushed past its training regime
keeps: the input-output patterns the original simulator shows, learned from a sample of runs
leaves_out: physical detail and edge cases outside the scenarios it was trained on
failure_boundary: gives plausible-looking answers for inputs it never saw during training, with no warning that they are wrong
everyday_anchor: A wind-tunnel test is expensive, so engineers build a faster stand-in model trained on a few real tests. They can now ask the model cheap questions—but only about wind speeds and shapes they already tested. Ask it about a speed or angle it has never seen, and it may invent an answer with total confidence.

title: Uncertainty And Generalization
common_problem: a prediction from a model is only useful if you know under which conditions you should actually trust it
why_it_matters: when scientific decisions cost lives or money, a model must be honest about its own edges and not guess past them—and most neural networks fail silently instead
keeps: error bounds, tests on shifted conditions, and explicit limits on training-data range
leaves_out: confidence in scenarios or physical regimes the model has never encountered before
failure_boundary: training error looks good while the model silently fails under new geometry, parameter range, sensor, or physical regime
everyday_anchor: A map is useful only if you know where it ends. Model uncertainty marks the edge of the map instead of pretending every road is known. When you leave the mapped territory, you must tell the decision-maker: I was trained here, not there.

title: Optimization For Learning
common_problem: models need a way to measure progress so they know which settings are better or worse
domain: turning model fitting into a repeatable computation
why_it_matters: adjusting weights downhill on the score works, but only for goals the score actually names; miss a goal and the model learns it wrong
keeps: a written score that measures how far the model's output is from the goal
leaves_out: anything the score didn't include in its list of things to improve
failure_boundary: the score goes down while the model learns wrong physics, if the score missed the real constraint
everyday_anchor: Think of a student revising an essay based on a teacher's rubric. The student improves whatever the rubric scores, but if the rubric forgets to check for logical flow, the essay can score high and still confuse readers. Optimization works the same way: the model improves only what the loss function measures.

title: Generative Modeling
common_problem: some tasks need many plausible examples, not a single best prediction, to explore what's possible
domain: creating plausible scientific samples, fields, or candidate designs
why_it_matters: it can explore a range of candidate fields or shapes when listing all possibilities is impossible; the catch is samples can look real yet violate the problem's rules
keeps: a learned rule that samples new outputs matching the patterns seen in training data
leaves_out: no check that generated samples obey physical laws, conservation rules, or task constraints
failure_boundary: a generated fluid flow looks smooth and realistic but conserves no mass; a design candidate is manufacturable in appearance but physically infeasible
everyday_anchor: A recipe can make countless cookies, all resembling the originals in flavor and texture. But if you skip the salt, they taste wrong even though they look perfect. Generative models are like that: they learn to make plausible-looking samples, but they don't automatically bake in whether those samples actually work for your real problem.

title: Graphs And Geometric Learning
common_problem: molecules, proteins, and meshes have a shape and connections that rows of numbers throw away
domain: systems made of interacting parts, meshes, molecules, or spatial relations
why_it_matters: treating a protein like a graph lets the model learn from neighborhood patterns instead of memorizing isolated points
keeps: dots and lines that show which parts touch, plus symmetries—flips and rotations that don't change the answer
leaves_out: distant effects that skip over neighbors, or interactions that only show up when the whole shape bends
failure_boundary: if the graph misses a real bond or connection, or if parts of the shape rearrange and the model sees a stranger structure
everyday_anchor: Imagine describing a city not as a list of addresses, but as a map of neighborhoods and roads—which blocks touch, which ones are far. A graph neural network learns that way: by looking at each atom's neighbors in a molecule, or each part of a protein's backbone touching nearby parts. The shape and order matter more than the raw count.

title: Neural Differential Equations
common_problem: scientists watch a system change over time but don't know the rule driving that change
domain: changing systems where time evolution is part of the model
why_it_matters: the time-stepping structure anchors learning in continuous evolution, keeping the idea that change is smooth, but mistakes in the learned rate compound over many steps and long predictions drift away
keeps: the continuous time-stepping structure paired with a learned prediction for the rate of change at each moment
leaves_out: guarantees the learned rate obeys boundary conditions or holds true far from the training data
failure_boundary: a small error in the learned rate, repeated over hundreds of time steps, pushes predictions into wildly wrong territory
everyday_anchor: Think of a GPS that guesses your speed. If it guesses right, step-by-step predictions land on the correct highway. But a small speed error, repeated mile after mile, eventually puts you in the wrong city. Neural differential equations have the same issue: tiny errors in the learned rate add up fast.

title: Symbolic Regression And Model Discovery
common_problem: a scientist may need a readable equation, not a numerical model that predicts but cannot be understood
domain: turning data into equations people can inspect
why_it_matters: a short equation lets you test new cases, argue about whether it makes sense, and reuse it in different settings—much harder with a large fitted model you cannot read
keeps: candidate formulas that can be written down, tested, compared, and shared with other scientists
leaves_out: unmeasured variables, physics the data never triggered, and formula terms no search explored
failure_boundary: a neat formula fits your lab's data perfectly but uses the wrong variables or breaks when conditions shift
everyday_anchor: Imagine you measured how fast plants grow and guessed the formula is 'height equals sunlight times water.' You scribble it down and test it on new plants in shadow—it fails. Symbolic regression does this: searches for formulas that fit your data, then lets you inspect them to see if they're actually sensible or just lucky on the numbers you collected.

title: Foundation Models For PDEs
common_problem: scientists train separate models for each PDE, each grid size, each parameter—expensive duplication
domain: broad families of PDE problems and scientific fields
why_it_matters: one shared model reduces training cost if it captures features that matter across tasks, but only if those features actually transfer
keeps: learned patterns that appear across many related equations and initial conditions
leaves_out: guarantee that training on old cases covers genuinely new boundary conditions or regimes
failure_boundary: the model trains on common cases and misses rare physical regimes, different boundary shapes, or unseen initial conditions
everyday_anchor: A weather forecaster trains once on years of temperature and wind patterns, then tries to predict a hurricane—a scenario outside the training set. The model learned weather's general shape but never saw that extreme case. Similarly, a foundation model for PDEs learns common flow or heat patterns, but a rare shock, a new material, or an edge condition can fool it.

title: Attention For Scientific Fields
common_problem: a local spot in a field may depend on faraway information, but scanning everywhere costs too much
domain: large scientific fields where distant parts may interact
why_it_matters: it lets the model move information across the field only where needed, trading speed for which distant interactions it can reach
keeps: the paths between distant parts that matter for the prediction
leaves_out: connections the attention pattern ignores or cannot see
failure_boundary: when attention weight patterns are wrong, the model skips over long-range effects that are essential to the physical quantity being predicted
everyday_anchor: Imagine a weather forecaster looking at a satellite image to predict rain at one city. She doesn't study every pixel equally—her eyes zoom to distant pressure systems and ocean temperatures that actually drive local weather. Attention works the same way: it weights which parts of the input field matter for each prediction, focusing computation on distant influences that truly connect.
